newsitem.title: ITALY: Benetton buys sister firm Sportsystem.
newsitem.headline: Benetton buys sister firm Sportsystem.

text.p: Italian clothing giant Benetton Tuesday announced its long-anticipated purchase of sister company Benetton Sportsystem, marking a radical change in the group's growth philosophy over its 32-year history.

The deal brings together Benetton, which sells through its 7,000 licensed retail outlets in 120 countries, with a company with several well-known brands such as Rollerblade selling through independent retail outlets.

Benetton is buying 57 percent of Benetton Sportsystem from the Benetton family holding company Edizione Holding for 318 billion lire ($182 million), and it will make an offer for the remaining 43 percent by March 31, 1998 with the payment of a further 249 billion lire ($142.5 million).

It added in a statement that Benetton Sportsystem had been valued at 560 billion lire ($320.5 million), but that Benetton will be paying slightly more for the whole company due to the delayed payment for the second 43 percent stake.
Benetton is 71.3 percent controlled by Edizione with its remaining shares quoted on the Milan stock market, while prior to this deal Benetton Sportsystem was wholly owned by Edizione.

The stock market had long awaited the deal by the company based in Ponzano in the Veneto region of northeast Italy, but analysts feared that Edizione would inflate the sale price of the money-losing Sportsystem to the cash-rich Benetton.
"From our point of view, we have done a good deal, having bought in a moment of weakness," Benetton Managing Director Carlo Gilardi told a news conference after the announcement.

Benetton Sportsystem boasts a number of leading sports brands such as Prince tennis racquets, Nordica ski boots, Rollerblade in-line skates, Kastle skis and bicyles, Killer Loop sportswear and Asolo mountain boots.

Benetton Sportsystem had 1996 sales of 1.246 trillion lire ($713.2 billion) in 1996, but registered a net loss of 14 billion lire ($8 billion) after making a small profit of 25 billion lire ($14.3 billion) in 1995.
Gilardi said Sportsystem was already returning to profit for 1997 and in a couple of years believed it would be reporting operating profit margins in the order of 8 percent.

Analysts said it may be difficult to link Benetton's unique system of manufacturing, commissioning agents and licensed retail outlets with Sportsystem, and said the only real synergies between the two groups would be in branded sportswear.
They said Sportsystem would dilute Benetton's margins and could be seen as a risky move after Benetton's history of steady organic growth, but others said it was a move Benetton needed.

Gilardi said Benetton's excess cash of 350 billion lire ($200.3 million) in 1997 and almost all of this would be used to finance the acquisition. After the purchase, Benetton said it will have a debt to equity ratio of under 30 percent.
Total global sales of the combined company will rise to 4.4 trillion lire ($2.5 billion), with the proportion of its sales from North America rising to around 20 percent of its total.
